  • paladeva’s ĪS has so far been interpreted mainly as an attempt to

  • splays many similarities with Utpaladeva’s short treatise as regards

  • fute them. By writing a text so blatantly at odds with his own
  • taphysical principles and so obviously relying on arguments put
  • rward by earlier authors, Utpaladeva probably meant to include Nyāya
  • ncepts within the scope of his system while presenting them as a lower
  • rspective; but it is also very likely that he primarily saw these
  • iyāyika arguments as the philosophical justification of the
  • iddhāntikas’ dualist understanding of the relationship between īśvara
  • d the Self. The ĪS can therefore be read as a message sent to the
  • iddhāntikas and emphasizing Utpaladeva’s philosophical solidarity as a
  • iva author (but also the capacity of non-dualism to integrate the

  • nting at the inferiority of the Saiddhāntikas’ metaphysics from the
  • timate viewpoint of non-dualism.
  • is point is of interest in the more general perspective of
  • paladeva’s relationship with the Śaiva Siddhānta. Modern scholarship

  • s background religious issues, most notably by avoiding to have
  • course to the authority of scriptures.166 But Utpaladeva’s attempt to
  • esent the metaphysical tenets of Śaiva non-dualism in the religiously
  • asi-neutral discourse of Brahmanico-Buddhist epistemological
  • ntroversies should not be interpreted as a sign that Utpaladeva lacked
  • terest in his Śaiva rivals’ metaphysics, first and foremost because
  • is attempt had a prestigious precedent in the Śaiva Siddhānta itself:
  • dyojyotis had already departed from mere scriptural exegesis by

  • ahmanical opponents, and in this respect the ĪPK seem to have been

  • nspicuously engaging in a dialogue with non-Śaiva authors, Utpaladeva
  • so sustained an implicit debate with the Saiddhāntikas that, however
  • screte, is perceptible for instance in the key passages of the

  • eations ascribed to yogins.

  • iddhāntikas: in his commentary on Sadyojyotis’ demonstration of God,
  • makaṇṭha apparently relies on some of the arguments found in the ĪS,
  • t he also seems to answer Utpaladeva’s criticism of the Saiddhāntika
  • tion of īśvara. Thus, as seen above, the ĪPKs oppose the idea that

  • owledge and action and those of the Lord, there is no difference of
  • ture between them, so that the individual’s experience of these powers
  • already the very experience of the Lord’s powers.168 In his
  • troduction to the second chapter of the NP, Rāmakaṇṭha presents a
  • milar objection: if the individual knows by mere self-awareness his
  • wers of knowledge and action, what is the point of demonstrating the
  • rd’s existence, and why did Sadyojyotis take the trouble of writing a
  • stinct chapter on the Lord once he had composed the chapter on the
  • dividual subject?169 Rāmakaṇṭha replies that contrary to the
  • dividual Self, the Lord is not known through mere self-awareness
  • ince the Self of the Lord and that of the individual are distinct) and
  • mains imperceptible, so that the Lord’s agency in the cosmic creation
  • st still be proved.170 With this answer, Rāmakaṇṭha seems to continue
  • e discrete dialogue initiated by Somānanda and Utpaladeva between the
  • iva Siddhānta and Śaiva non-dualism – a dialogue that remains largely
  • explored, and on which a comparative study of the demonstrations of
  • e Self by Utpaladeva and Rāmakaṇṭha for instance171 could certainly
  • ed some light.

  • Although the fifty-six stanzas of the ĪS and the Vr̥tti thereon have
  • oused little scholarly interest so far, two important studies must be
  • ntioned in this respect: Taber 1986, which summarizes the whole
  • eatise and offers a very insightful philosophical analysis of it; and
  • asser 2002, an excellent study of the Indian controversy over the
  • istence of God that contains (pp. 149-58) a translation and analysis
  • some key passages in the ĪS.
  • In the context of the proof of īśvara, the term “God” might seem most
  • propriate to the Western reader. Nonetheless I have kept the more
  • teral term “Lord” in the translations at least, because īśvara
  • signates first and foremost a person who has power or reigns over
  • mething (see, for example, ĪPVV III: 181-82: yatra yad āyattaṁ sa
  • treśvaro rājeva nije rājye . . . “That on which something depends is
  • e Lord of this [thing], as a king [who is the Lord] of his kingdom . .
  • ), and the various Indian authors quoted below often use the term in
  • is sense (for an example of this use by Praśastapāda, see Chemparathy
  • 68: 84; cf. e.g. Rāmakaṇṭha’s assertion that the potter is īśvara with
  • spect to the pot in KV, p. 73).
  • See Taber 1986: 106-07; Krasser 2002: 149-50.
  • Abhinavagupta repeatedly calls the supporters of Utpaladeva’s doctrine
  • e “proponents of the non-duality with the Lord” (īśvarādvayavādin):
  • e e.g. ĪPVV II: 122 or 129 (quoted in Ratié 2011a: 385, n 44 and
  • 8-99, n 64). This non-duality is primarily to be understood as the
  • entity of the individual’s Self (ātman) with the Lord, but also as the
  • solute ontological dependence of the phenomenal world on īśvara
  • nceived as an all-encompassing consciousness that creates the universe
  • rely by taking on its various forms.
  • See e.g. Taber 1986: 107; Torella 1994: 40; Krasser 2002: 151ff.
  • ĪS: 1: tanukaraṇādikāryaṁ buddhimatkartr̥pūrvakaṁ
  • nniveśa-viśeṣavattvāt, yad yat sanniveśaviśeṣavat tat tad
  • ddhimatkartr̥nirmitaṁ yathā ghaṭaḥ, buddhimatkartr̥pūrvakaṁ yan na
  • avati na tat sanniveśaviśeṣavatkāryaṁ yathā paramāṇvākāśaśaśaviṣāṇādi,
  • thā ca bhavati sanniveśaviśeṣavat tanvādikāryam, tasmād
  • ddhimatkartr̥pūrvakam iti. “An effect such as bodies, organs and so on
  • esupposes an intelligent agent (buddhimatkartr̥), because it possesses
  • specific arrangement (sanniveśaviśeṣa). Whatever has a specific
  • rangement was created by an intelligent agent – a pot for instance
  • as created by a potter; whereas] that which does not presuppose an
